Senses.Note: A wine-lees-guzzling fellow is a cutting person-appraisal. Huangbo applies it to noisy, second-hand seekers; later speakers raise the insult, redirect it at Shakyamuni, or turn it on their own assembly.

Senses.Explanation: A wine-lees-guzzling fellow lives on what remains after the drink rather than the wine itself. Huangbo makes the insult a public verdict on seekers who chase crowded reputations and stored words; later speakers preserve that second-hand edge while changing its target. Huangbo Xiyun drives the assembly and specifies the conduct his insult attacks: noisy crowds, easy travel, and learned words without the tested person. Xutang Zhiyu raises the whole exchange and warns against stopping at the insulting phrase itself. Pingzi Chulin and Daochang Juhui redirect the verdict at Shakyamuni in separate hall addresses; Sanyi Mingyu directs it at his own assembly.

Senses.Note: The nominal phrase asks for or identifies a remarkable matter. Duplicate recensions of the Baizhang and Ananda cases are each counted once, not as independent dialogues.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase names a remarkable or extraordinary matter. An unnamed monk asks Qingya whether anything more exceptional exists; one repeatedly transmitted Baizhang dialogue asks what the remarkable matter is. Ananda calls what he saw in the city a remarkable event; Yuanwu Keqin praises the flourishing of the community as a remarkable matter; another quoted monk asks Deshan for the Chan tradition’s remarkable matter. Zhe'an Jingfan raises the question himself before answering with a winter scene; Miaofeng Zhishan answers it with 'the crape-myrtle gentleman beneath the crape-myrtle blossoms.'

Senses.Explanation: The isolated four graphs say, 'stop (歇)—that is (即) awakening (菩提),' but the corpus's recurring full quotation supplies the omitted subject: 'the crazed mind does not stop; when it stops, that is awakening' (狂心不歇，歇即菩提). A historical compendium follows the phrase with its own explicit explanation, beginning 'as for “when it stops, that is awakening”' and describing what it calls awakening. Chan masters repeatedly take up the quoted line in hall discourse. One says that when dust-labor suddenly stops, 'when it stops, that is awakening,' then immediately asks the assembly, 'from where is it obtained?' Another says people run north, south, east, and west for years without a place to stop and asks, 'can you people stop?' The Zen deviation is the quotation's use as a public teaching-seat proposition and direct question. Restoring its attested subject avoids turning every kind of ceasing into the roadmap's broad 'ceasing itself is enlightenment.'
